clinicalPearls: Aeromonas species are Gram-negative bacilli widespread in fresh and brackish water, soil and aquatic animals
The two commonest syndromes are watery or dysenteric gastroenteritis and wound infection following freshwater exposure or injury
Classic wound scenarios include lacerations sustained in lakes or rivers and infections after therapeutic or accidental leech application
Soft-tissue infection can progress from cellulitis to necrotising fasciitis and myonecrosis, particularly in immunocompromised or cirrhotic patients
Bacteraemia occurs mainly in hosts with liver disease or malignancy and may be rapidly progressive
Many isolates produce inducible beta-lactamases, so fluoroquinolones, third-generation cephalosporins, aminoglycosides or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole are commonly used, guided by susceptibility
Necrotising soft-tissue disease requires prompt surgical debridement in addition to antibiotics
reference.pathophysiology: Aeromonas organisms are ubiquitous aquatic bacteria that cause disease after ingestion of contaminated water or food, or through direct wound inoculation from freshwater or aquatic animals such as leeches and fish. They elaborate a range of virulence factors, including cytotoxic and haemolytic enterotoxins, proteases and adhesins, which disrupt intestinal epithelium to cause diarrhoea and degrade soft tissue to produce spreading cellulitis and necrosis. In hosts with impaired defences, particularly those with chronic liver disease or malignancy, the organism can invade the bloodstream, and its production of inducible beta-lactamases contributes to treatment difficulty.
additionalDifferentials: Vibrio vulnificus wound infection and sepsis
Group A streptococcal or clostridial necrotising soft-tissue infection
Bacterial gastroenteritis from Salmonella, Shigella or Campylobacter
Other Gram-negative bacteraemia in the cirrhotic patient
additionalInvestigations: Stool culture on selective media in diarrhoeal illness
Culture of wound aspirate, tissue or blood in soft-tissue and systemic disease
Gram stain of exudate showing Gram-negative bacilli
Antimicrobial susceptibility testing given inducible beta-lactamase production
Imaging of the affected soft tissues to assess depth and necrosis
Liver function tests and assessment for immunosuppression to identify risk factors
redFlags: Rapidly spreading cellulitis with bullae or crepitus after freshwater or leech exposure
Sepsis in a patient with cirrhosis or malignancy following aquatic contact
Severe or bloody diarrhoea with dehydration
Imaging or operative findings of necrotising fasciitis
reference.prognosis: Self-limited gastroenteritis and localised wound infections generally do well, whereas necrotising soft-tissue disease and bacteraemia in immunocompromised hosts carry significant mortality without prompt antibiotics and surgery.
pitfalls: Overlooking Aeromonas in wound infections related to leech therapy
Empirical use of aminopenicillins that are typically ineffective
Underestimating the speed of soft-tissue progression in vulnerable hosts
Failing to obtain cultures before starting antibiotics
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Treat established infection with a fluoroquinolone, third-generation cephalosporin, aminoglycoside or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, guided by susceptibility testing
Avoid reliance on penicillins and early-generation cephalosporins because inducible beta-lactamases render them unreliable
Manage self-limiting gastroenteritis mainly with oral or intravenous rehydration, reserving antibiotics for severe, dysenteric or prolonged illness and immunocompromised hosts
Undertake urgent surgical debridement for necrotising fasciitis or myonecrosis alongside broad-spectrum antibiotics
Provide sepsis resuscitation and source control for bacteraemia, particularly in cirrhotic or immunocompromised patients
Send wound, tissue or blood cultures with susceptibility testing to direct and de-escalate therapy
Assess and address host risk factors such as chronic liver disease, malignancy and immunosuppression
